standfirst: A modern chef falls into Joseon and ends up cooking for a tyrant who is only dangerous when the food is bad. For four episodes the dishes are worth the eighty minute runtime and Lee Chae Min is the best new thing in a sageuk this year. Then the show works out that it has twelve long hours and no story, and the plates start getting more attention than the people. These picks are the timeslip and food romances that hold up better.

picks.why: The same premise with an actual script. A modern person dropped into a Joseon palace, a royal kitchen as a battlefield, court factions treating food and favour as currency. Same comedy, better plotted, and the political half genuinely pays off. Difference: the humour is much broader and the back half turns dark, so it is less of a pleasant meal and more of a story.

If the food was the reason: a chef, a restaurateur, and cooking shot as the main event rather than the backdrop. Same appetite for watching somebody be brilliant with ingredients. Difference: it is a contemporary romance with no fantasy premise, and it falls apart even harder in its final third, peaking at episode four and dropping three full points.

The 2026 sageuk that does what this one only gestures at: comedy, romance and court politics all working at once, across sixteen episodes that actually resolve. Same register, no timeslip. Difference: the heroine's skill is medicine and theft rather than cooking, and the class danger is real, so there is jeopardy where this show has recipes.

For the palace with a fantasy element and a woman who does not belong there. Same easy tone, same reliance on a charismatic royal and a heroine with a gift. Difference: the fantasy is possession rather than time travel, it runs to sixteen episodes on a twelve episode story, and the romance is softer and slower.

The palace romance where the woman has something to lose by accepting. Same period, better history, much more disciplined about what a king can and cannot do. Difference: it is a restrained tragedy with no comedy and no fantasy, so it asks for patience this show never demands.

A woman surviving Joseon on borrowed identity and applied intelligence. Same pleasure in watching a heroine outthink a system built to crush her. Difference: it is dark, with real torture and real consequence, and the food, comedy and fluttering that carry Bon Appetit are entirely missing.

against.title: Alchemy of Souls
against.why: The default fantasy sageuk pick, handed out for anything in a hanbok with a supernatural premise. It is a two part epic with a mythology to maintain and a cliffhanger instead of an ending. This is a twelve hour cooking show with a king in it. Anyone coming here expecting worldbuilding will be very confused by episode three.

against.title: Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo
against.why: Paired for the timeslip, and it is the tonal opposite. That show spends twenty episodes taking things away and its reputation is built on how much the ending hurts. Bon Appetit never risks anything. Following one with the other is a category error.

against.title: Twinkling Watermelon
against.why: Suggested as the other recent timeslip about a person out of their era, and the resemblance stops there. That one is a youth drama about family and music with a real emotional argument at its centre. This uses time travel as a delivery mechanism for a romance. Different genre, different intent.
